ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A smooth curved trough with mass $3m$ is at rest on a smooth horizontal ground, with its bottom smoothly connected to the horizontal surface. A small ball with mass $m$ slides down from a height $h$ on the trough, starting from rest. When the ball reaches the right wall, it collides with the vertical wall and bounces back with the same speed. The gravitational acceleration is given as $g$.

1. What is the magnitude of the velocity of the small ball when it first collides with the wall?
2. What is the maximum height that the small ball reaches when it slides up the curved groove again?

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: A smooth curved trough with mass $3m$ is at rest on a smooth horizontal ground, with its bottom smoothly connected to the horizontal surface. A small ball with mass $m$ slides down from a height $h$ on the trough, starting from rest. When the ball reaches the right wall, it collides with the vertical wall and bounces back with the same speed. The gravitational acceleration is given as $g$. 1. What is the magnitude of the velocity of the small ball when it first collides with the wall? 2. What is the maximum height that the small ball reaches when it slides up the curved groove again?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The two attached figures show the same physical device: on the left there is a section of smooth curved groove, smoothly connected downward from the position whose height is marked as h to the bottom horizontal plane; the small ball is located at a higher place of the curved groove and is ready to slide down; the bottom is a smooth horizontal plane, and there is a vertical wall at the right end; after the small ball reaches the right wall, it will rebound. Reasoning: let the magnitude of the velocity of the small ball in the ground reference frame before it first hits the right wall be u, and the velocity of the groove be V. During the process in which the small ball slides down from height h to the horizontal bottom and leaves the curved groove, the system composed of the ball and the groove has no external force impulse in the horizontal direction, so horizontal momentum is conserved: m u + 3m V = 0, therefore V = -u/3. Mechanical energy is conserved: mgh = (1/2)m u^2 + (1/2)(3m)V^2. Substituting V = -u/3 gives mgh = (1/2)m u^2 + (1/6)m u^2 = (2/3)m u^2, so u^2 = 3gh/2, hence u = sqrt(6gh)/2. After the small ball collides with the vertical wall on the right side, it reverses direction with the same speed, and its velocity is -u, while the groove still moves with V = -u/3. The small ball returns and, after entering the curved groove again, climbs upward. Taking the process from when the small ball has just returned to the bottom and enters the curved groove to the highest point, use horizontal momentum conservation for the ball and the groove: the initial momentum is m(-u)+3m(-u/3) = -2mu. When the small ball reaches the highest point relative to the curved groove, the ball and the groove have a common velocity U in the horizontal direction, so 4mU = -2mu, giving U = -u/2. Energy is conserved: the initial kinetic energy is (1/2)m u^2 + (1/2)(3m)(u/3)^2 = (2/3)m u^2; the final-state energy is mgH + (1/2)(4m)U^2 = mgH + (1/2)m u^2. Thus mgH = (2/3)m u^2 - (1/2)m u^2 = (1/6)m u^2. Substituting again u^2 = 3gh/2, we obtain H = h/4.
